name: Procurement Management Plan
purpose: A component of the project management plan that describes how all aspects of a procurement are managed and the activities done during the procurement process. It covers how the contractor's work integrates with the project, key dates, performance metrics, roles and authority, assumptions and constraints, legal terms, independent estimates, risk protection and prequalified sellers. It is developed once and does not usually change.

elements.guidance: How procured work is coordinated and integrated with the rest of the project, across the five areas below. The blank form prints a table with columns Area and Integration Approach and the five areas as fixed rows.
How the contractor's WBS will integrate with the project WBS.
How the contractor's schedule will integrate with the project schedule, including milestones and long lead items.
How contractor documentation will integrate with project documentation.
How risk identification, analysis and response will integrate with risk management for the overall project.
How the contractor's status reports will integrate with the project status report.

The timetable of key procurement activities, for example when the statement of work will be complete, when procurement documents are released and when proposals are due. The blank form prints Date and Activity columns.
The metrics used to evaluate the seller's performance. The blank form prints Item, Metric and Measurement Method columns; Table 2.33 does not describe a measurement method.
The roles, responsibilities and authority level of the project manager, the contractor and the procurement department, and any other significant stakeholder for the contract.
The assumptions and constraints that relate to the procurement activities. The blank form prints Category and Assumption/Constraint columns.
The location with legal jurisdiction and the currency for pricing and payment.
Whether independent cost estimates will be used and whether they are needed for source selection.
Requirements for performance bonds or insurance contracts to reduce risk.
Any prequalified sellers that will be used. The blank form prints four numbered lines.

tailoring: A project done with internal resources only needs no procurement management plan.
A project that buys materials under a standing purchase order with a vendor does not need one either.
For a project with a few procurements, consider combining this form with the procurement strategy (2.38).
The assumptions and constraints for procurements can be combined with the assumption log.
Work with the contracting or legal department so the plan complies with organisational purchasing policies.

notes: Blank form: PDF pages 161 to 162 (printed pages 150 to 151). Table 2.33 has 8 rows, with the first (Procurement integration) holding five sub-rows, so elements lists the parent and each sub-row; the blank form prints the sub-rows as the fixed rows of one table. The typical-information list names four integration areas (scope, schedule, documentation, risk) but Table 2.33 and the blank form add Reporting. The blank form prints Date, not Date Prepared. Prose labels differ from the blank form (Timing, Roles responsibilities and authority, Prequalified sellers); the blank form wins. The prose gives no guidance on choosing metrics, bonds or sellers beyond the descriptions above: not stated in the book. 'Scope baseline', 'Project team assignments' and 'Project budget' are not single forms and are named, not numbered. The alignment 'what_must_agree' texts are reading aids, since the book states only 'aligned and consistent'.
